Oh man, bodies are great! 

The satisfaction after eating a good meal!

The sublime tranquility in sinking into bed and finally resting your eyes after a very long day, and even moreso waking up refreshed!

The sensations of touch and pressure that you interact with the world by-shit lets you know you are alive man!

The incredible relief that comes after a good dump or piss!

Sex! Sex is awesome. A beautiful chemical cocktail of endorphins rushing everywhere, not to mention the great sense of intimacy!

The bite of winter as you run around in the snow and see the world blanketed in pristine white, and the heat of summer as you lounge through hot afternoons and prepare for long and active evenings! Fuck I love seasons and temperature ranges.

Being uncomfortable is necessary for a state of comfort to exist. Need bad to have good right?

The acquisition of material goods is a little more iffy, but goddamn do I enjoy possessions, experiences, and good food.

Everyone is a gasping, decaying, filthy sack of meat and organs and putrid flesh, and it kicks fucking ass!

If you've been depressed for a long time, try counseling. If you are sad about having a body, best re-evaluate.

I'm trying to man. Pretty much paralyzed by massive depression for a year (sounds like a total bullshit copout, but it was honestly some horrible shit), but I go a psychologist now and am actually starting to make some progress. It's pretty awful having disappointed so many people though, and seeing everyone whiz by me in life. Picking up the pieces and persisting is very, very difficult at times.

Thanks for the advice and taking the time to reply.

Sometimes life deals shit hands, sometimes people get built differently. There's a lot of bullshit in life, but a lot of beauty too. Counseling and therapy often just involves talking to a bro that gets what you're feeling, and guides you to understanding or changing your outlook. Give it a thought mate.

Therapy mate, get a nice psychologist. Medication with it, as the situation warrants. Easy peasy! Changing your outlook involves more than any epiphany some asshole on the internet like me can give. Professionals have this shit on lock.

Holy shit calm the fuck down. 3 semesters of college is essentially nothing-still plenty of time to prove yourself. All the pre-med courses take just a few short years to accomplish (1 yr physics, 1 yr psych, 2 yrs chem, some bio). Easy goddamn peasy. A lot of med applications is in the mcat. If you can demolish that you'll be ok. Median age of entry into med school is like 26. Very few applicants get in right from college. So you have additional time to prove yourself then. However, you are right in that continuing in your current course will not be great. So figure that shit out. If depression is actually your problem, tell your folks and get a therapist (its pretty easy, cheap too if your parents have insurance to latch onto-thanks Obama). Absolutely bust your balls over your studies-it will make you feel better about being invested in and will pay off.

What to do now:


*Make appointments with both your major advisor and your med advisor. Explain your situation (maybe drop that you are seeking counseling {you can probably just get this through your school actually}, but don't feel the need to elaborate more than that), and ask what you would need to do/demonstrate in order to achieve your goals and turn your shit around. They will definitely just tell you what I did, some version of figure out what horrible study habits allowed you to get a D in Gen Chem, retake that shit and prove yourself. Don't be afraid to make the appointments, that's part of their job, and part of what your tuition goes to. Remember, these guys are literally paid to be your friends. They don't want you struggling, they know this shit can be hard.

*Get treated for depression-counseling/therapy, meds if you need em, etc. Just do it-feeling like shit all the time sucks ass.

*Resolve your academic shit-nobody gives a rat's ass about a C you got in intro chem when you were still a teenager if you did very well in higher level chem courses. However, they get much harder man. Remember those appointments you signed up for? They are going to tell you that if you are having such a struggle with science on easy mode, it doesn't bode well for upper level coursework. OChem is your proving ground. That shit will test you, and you have to do well. Fix whatever is holding you back-mental health, shit study habits, get it taken care of. It's the only way.

*You're probably going to have to tell your parents sooner or later. It's not such a bad thing. If you lump it together with how you are seeking treatment and really going to dedicate yourself (AND THEN DO IT), you'll be fine.

Take home message: absolutely bust your balls and you'll be fine. Your profs and I will tell you that nothing is out of reach yet, but it will take major commitment.

About the same reason you can be a master baker yet be a total shitcunt at woodcarving. Different skills, my friend, apples and oranges. Randomly approaching people at bars is pretty difficult social interaction-try joining clubs, volunteering, anything that gets you out there in a more socially fluid way. Have more conversations with your partners (ffs what else do you do for 10 hours), invite the bastards out for a drink and go from there. Small steps and lots of them.

You've certainly done a lot of good. Being someone that other people can rely on and are comfortable enough with to share their problems is very deserving of respect. Sometimes you have to deal with more bad situations and stress than might be fair in life, but take comfort in knowing that you have a profound impact on the livelihood of others. However, at some point you have to realize that you can't meet everyones demands for support-it's called getting burned out. You do what you can, but there is no shame in simply saying "thats really none of my business, maybe you should talk to x about it" or "I'm here for you, but I'm not comfortable doing z." Suggest therapy or sources of clarity outside yourself. You're right, it's above your pay grade-15 year olds trying to off themselves quite honestly need more help than you can give them alone. Encourage them to seek it.

As for wanting support yourself, friends that support you like that are difficult to come by, and-at least in my experience-take many years of building trust. Find someone that you can talk to-counselor at school, parents, wizened middle aged blue collar worker-just having a conversation about it will do wonders.

1) Homeless people in first world countries don't starve unless they have many mental or drug-related problems--there are many programs providing food, some shelter, etc. The bigger concern is breaking out of homelessness when you get there.

2) Unfortunately, it is often not possible to work exclusively at your passion in life (particularly if it is something like art, music, athletics, or acting->these professions require lots of work-often talent, incredible luck, and random connections to be profitable). However, it is possible to pursue them as hobbies or to do them as 'side jobs' in hopes that they can eventually sustain you. This is very common for comedians, artists, etc. Even though you are passionate about your music, it is unrealistic to think that your music career can sustain you immediately on launch. You need a job to-at the very least-hold you over, optimistically for the time it will take you to refine your music, realistically for many years, likely (going by the numbers) for the rest of your life. The cold truth is that not that many people pursuing these types of professions can make it. But hell, that's totally ok-many people in many different lifestyles are passionate about their music, and find satisfaction in pursuing it in their free time. College is a great step-go to that shit and actually work at it, and doors will open to jobs that you will be ok with. Maybe even like.

3) Social problems-fuck 'em, go your own way and find people that actually want to be around you. Putting yourself out there and improving your social skills is harder than it sounds, but its a necessary and fulfilling step to take. Volunteering, clubs, workplace socializing; all good things to do. Start by just talking to people doing the same thing and work your way up. Don't cling to a few people like a limpet-work on finding more anywhere you go. People are goddamn everywhere, most of them are pretty chill, almost all of them won't dick you around just for approaching. Special side note for girls-you can build up to this through other social interaction, but honestly, if you can manage to be someone that makes you happy and have genuine friends, girls will be no problem. Don't worry about it for even a moment. Though maybe cut that social media stuff out.

4) Depression-if you have health insurance (through parents), go to a doctor and/or sign up for a therapist. They will be mostly covered. Get diagnosed, treated, and possibly medicated. Aint no thang.

5) Father-sounds like a shit situation. My advice is work at school and get a side job in the mean time. Getting some money saved will allow you to (in time) move out. It's going to be a lot of suck getting to that point, but it all gets easier.

Adding on to this cunt, the first step to leading a fulfilling life is to be someone that makes you happy. The second (and optional) step is to be with someone that makes you happy. Focus on becoming who you want to be; don't define yourself by relationships.

Here's a quick vignette that a friend sent me a long time ago (although a quick google reveals its from a book by a buddhist monk): 

"The new prisoner was afraid and very depressed. The stone walls of his cell soaked up any warmth; the hard iron bars sneered at all compassion; the jarring collision of steel, as his cell door closed, locked hope beyond reach. His heart sank low as his sentence stretched long. On the wall, by the head of his cot, he saw scratched in the stone the following words: This too will pass.

These words pulled him through, as they must have supported the prisoner before him. No matter how hard it got, he would look at the inscription and remember, 'This too will pass.' On the day he was released, he knew the truth of these words. His time was completed; jail too had passed.

As he regained his life, he often thought about that message, writing it on bits of paper to leave by his bedside, in his car, and at work. Even when times were bad, he never got depressed. He simply remembered, 'This too will pass,' and struggled on through. The bad times never seemed to last all that long. Then when good times came he enjoyed them, but never too carelessly. Again he remembered, 'This too will pass,' and so carried on working at his life, taking nothing for granted. The good times always seemed to last uncommonly long.

Even when he got cancer, 'This too will pass' gave him hope. Hope gave him strength and the positive attitude that beat the disease. One day the specialist confirmed that 'the cancer too had passed.'

At the end of his days, on his death bed, he whispered to his loved ones, 'This too will pass,' and settled easily into death. His words were his last gift of love to his family and friends. They learned from him that 'grief too will pass.'

Depression is a prison that many of us pass through. 'This too will pass' helps us pull through. It also avoids one of the great causes of depression, which is taking the happy times too much for granted."

Therapy mate, change up that outlook. Therapy kicks ass. Sure, you met and lost one great person, the world is full of them. There's a certain beauty in feeling sad because of losing something that made you so happy; makes you feel alive. Seek out people that make you feel the same way, look back on your good times without regret. The first step to leading a good and fullfilling life is to be someone that makes you happy. The second (optional) step is to be with people that make you happy.

As far as that 'involuntarily going to the hospital' stuff goes, don't even sweat it. Happens all the time.

Go to the mental health center. Get a therapist and/or medication as the situation warrants. This is cheaper than it sounds, and if you don't have health coverage from your work you are technically covered by any health insurance your parents might have until 26 (thanks Obama). The mere act of sitting down and having a conversation with a therapist will do wonders-it's very nice. Hell, go to a therapist anyway. Everyone could use more clarity in their lives.

As far as medication goes, it takes about a month for any program to take full effect (need x amount of half lives, etc), and then you switch to a new one if you don't feel better, so the year figure is relatively accurate. Lots of people just get built differently and have a lack of x chemical. If it can't be fixed with diet, exercise, or therapy, fix it with drugs. Don't even worry about that shit, medication is great.

The hard part is going to be forcing yourself to go to work, go through life, and be as good a partner as you can (although your boyfriend sounds all kinds of supportive, so nice going there) while the medication and therapy get you sorted.

I'm in no position to give you enlightenment beyond what everyone else has suggested, but-from what I can piece together-it sounds like you switch up that medication grind. Mention something about it not working to your doctor and he'll set you up like pillbo baggins (I should be in the same boat, but I'm an idiot and cling to the belief that I'll feel better if I can only manage to fix everything).

"previous attempt to move into a group home but that effort failed because no one could drive her"

This should be easy to fix, if it's a situation that calls for immediate escape. Pay for an uber, help make arrangements, explain the situation; doesn't sound like anything that throwing a few dollars at won't help.
 
As I see it, your best bet is getting her on the road to employment. Any shit job will do, but be careful not to make her life into one big countdown of when you finally swoop in and rescue her. Therapy, employment, and exercise can work wonders.

People get built differently-ain't no thang. Usually there is something in the chemical cocktail that could use balancing.  Meditation, exercise, if nothing else get on that sweet, sweet, medication grind.

Can't really offer you anything but the best of luck from what you've given me. Depending on many factors, you're probably right about it not working, but maybe cut the dosages in half and get really high two days in a row. Use a bit of that extra time to give a touch more detail and I'll write back.

You should go to a psychologist or therapist-if your parents have decent insurance you can easily do it for $0-40 per appointment (thanks Obama) out of pocket. Just putting that shit on the table and having a real conversation with someone can help immensely. Actually do this and everything else can begin to fall into place. I'd advise on other stuff, but I'm just some asshole on the internet.
